title: The Ecliptic: The Planets’ Highway
objective: After this level you can explain why the Sun, Moon and planets all travel along the same narrow band of sky.
summary: The ecliptic is the Sun’s yearly path. The Moon and planets stay near it because the solar system is flat.

cards.headline: The planets don’t roam the whole sky. They stick to one narrow road.
The Sun’s yearly path
cards.body: As Earth orbits, the Sun seems to drift slowly against the background stars, returning to the same spot after a year. The line it traces is called the ecliptic. The zodiac constellations lie along it, though it also crosses a 13th constellation, Ophiuchus.
cards.callout: Ecliptic = the Sun’s path over a year

cards.headline: A flat solar system
cards.body: The planets all orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane, and the Moon orbits Earth close to it too. Seen from inside that plane, we see everything strung along one line: the ecliptic. Spot a bright “star” near where the Sun set? Check if it’s a planet.

cards.fact: Eclipses can only happen when the Moon is on the ecliptic.
cards.context: The Moon’s orbit is tilted slightly, so most months it passes just above or below the Sun’s path. Only when it crosses the ecliptic at the right moment do we get an eclipse.

cards.headline: Planetary highway: mapped
learned: The ecliptic is the Sun’s path over a year
The planets stay near it because the solar system is flat
Eclipses need the Moon on the ecliptic

options.label: The line of Earth’s equator projected onto the sky
options.rationale: That’s the celestial equator, a different line.

options.label: The path the Moon’s shadow takes across Earth
options.rationale: Shadows cause eclipses; the ecliptic is the Sun’s path.

options.label: The Sun’s apparent path across the sky over a year
The band of the Milky Way across the night sky
options.rationale: The ecliptic is set by Earth’s orbit.

questions.explanation: Over a year, the Sun appears to move against the stars along a line called the ecliptic.

questions.prompt: Why do the planets always appear near the ecliptic?

options.label: They are pulled toward the Sun’s path by the stars
options.rationale: Distant stars have no such effect.

options.label: Their orbits lie in nearly the same flat plane as Earth’s
The ecliptic is where the sky is darkest
options.rationale: Darkness has nothing to do with it.

options.label: They orbit Earth along that line
options.rationale: Planets orbit the Sun, not Earth.

questions.explanation: The solar system is flat: the planets orbit in nearly the same plane as Earth, so from Earth they all appear close to the Sun’s path.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: there’s a new Moon every month. Why isn’t there a solar eclipse every month?

options.label: The Moon is too far away to cover the Sun most months
options.rationale: It’s the tilt of the Moon’s orbit, not its distance, that usually prevents it.

options.label: Solar eclipses can only happen in the summer months
options.rationale: Eclipses can happen in any season.

options.label: Earth’s shadow blocks the Moon’s shadow most months
options.rationale: In a solar eclipse it’s the Moon’s shadow that matters.

options.label: The Moon usually passes just above or below the Sun’s path

questions.explanation: The Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted to the ecliptic. Most new Moons pass above or below the Sun; only a line-up on the ecliptic gives a solar eclipse.
